title: Lumbar decompression for cauda equina syndrome
subtitle: Discectomy with laminotomy or laminectomy

sources.org: Society of British Neurological Surgeons (SBNS) and British Association of Spine Surgeons (BASS)
sources.title: Standards of care for investigation and management of cauda equina syndrome

sources.org: Getting It Right First Time (GIRFT), NHS England
sources.title: National suspected cauda equina syndrome (CES) pathway

indications: Cauda equina syndrome with radiological compression of the cauda equina, most often a large central lumbar disc prolapse.
Both incomplete CES and CES with retention, as soon as possible after confirmation.
contraindications: No compression on MRI. Look for another cause rather than operating.
Uncorrected coagulopathy: correct urgently in parallel.
Compression from tumour, infection or haematoma needs a different operative plan.
preparation: MRI reviewed in theatre: level, side of the disc, canal size, and any sequestrated fragment.
Record the pre-operative neurological, saddle sensation and bladder status with the time.
Catheter in situ if in retention.
Consent should include dural tear and CSF leak, nerve root injury, failure to recover bladder, bowel or sexual function, infection, haematoma, recurrence and wrong level.
positioning: Prone on a frame or bolsters that keep the abdomen free, to reduce epidural venous bleeding.
Pad the eyes, face, breasts, genitals and bony prominences; no pressure on the orbits.
Slight flexion opens the interlaminar window.
equipment: Kerrison rongeurs, pituitary rongeurs, nerve root retractor, dissectors.
anatomy: The cauda equina occupies the thecal sac below the conus, usually from L1 or L2.
A large central disc compresses the whole thecal sac. Room to retract the sac is limited, which is why a wider bony decompression is often needed.
The traversing root runs over the disc at its level and exits at the level below; the exiting root lies higher in the foramen.
Epidural veins bleed readily when the abdomen is compressed.
criticalSafety: Confirm the level radiologically before incising and again before opening the canal.
Do not retract a tightly compressed thecal sac to reach the disc; create room by removing bone first.
Confirm free movement of the thecal sac and roots at the end.
structuresAtRisk: Great vessels anterior to the disc if instruments pass through the anterior annulus
Pars interarticularis and facet joints if over-resected
commonErrors: Wrong-level surgery from inadequate imaging confirmation.
Forceful retraction of a compressed thecal sac.
Inserting pituitary rongeurs too deep through the anterior annulus.
complications: Persisting bladder, bowel or sexual dysfunction, or saddle anaesthesia.
postop: Document post-operative lower-limb, saddle and bladder function as a baseline.
Urgent MRI for new deficit or new retention: post-operative epidural haematoma must be excluded.
Trial without catheter and post-void residual scan; urology referral for persisting dysfunction.
Follow-up for bladder, bowel, sexual and psychological effects, with written information.

steps.emphasis: The spinal level and side are read from the MRI aloud and matched to the mark.
Prone with the abdomen free; this reduces epidural venous bleeding more than any haemostatic agent.
Only if a durotomy has occurred; tell the ward team and record the plan.
Send disc material for histology if there is any suspicion of tumour or infection.
Include saddle sensation and bladder function in the baseline and the trigger.

step.spine.level-check.title: Radiological level confirmation
step.spine.level-check.why: Wrong-level spinal surgery is a recognised never-event pattern. Counting from the sacrum on the image intensifier, before and after exposure, is the only reliable protection.
how: Place a marker at the planned level and screen in the lateral view before incision.
Count from the sacrum, and account for transitional vertebrae seen on the MRI.
Re-check with an instrument on the lamina once exposed, before removing bone.
pitfalls: Relying on palpation of spinous processes alone.

step.spine.exposure.title: Midline exposure and laminotomy
step.spine.exposure.why: Adequate bony access creates space to reach the disc without retracting a compressed thecal sac.
how: Midline incision over the level, subperiosteal dissection of the paraspinal muscles off the lamina.
Remove the inferior part of the upper lamina and the ligamentum flavum with Kerrison rongeurs.
Extend to a full laminectomy if the disc is large and central and the sac cannot be mobilised safely.
pitfalls: Removing so much facet that the segment becomes unstable.

step.spine.decompress.title: Discectomy and decompression of the thecal sac
step.spine.decompress.why: This is the step that relieves the compression. It must be done without adding traction injury to roots already under pressure.
how: Identify the thecal sac and the traversing root; retract gently only once there is room.
Coagulate epidural veins, incise the annulus, and remove the herniated disc and free fragments.
Keep pituitary rongeurs at a controlled depth within the disc space.
structuresAtRisk: Great vessels anterior to the disc
pitfalls: Pushing instruments through the anterior annulus into the retroperitoneum.

step.spine.confirm.title: Confirming adequate decompression
step.spine.confirm.why: The operation is judged by the space left for the cauda equina. A retained fragment means a second operation and a worse outcome.
how: Check that the thecal sac is slack and re-expands, and that the roots move freely.
Probe under the sac, into the foramen and up and down the canal for retained fragments.
Inspect the dura for any tear before closing.
pitfalls: Stopping when the obvious fragment is out, leaving a migrated piece behind.
